title: This Old Dollar Store Is Now a Free Store — and a Roller Rink!
summary:
Imagine walking into an old store covered in graffiti. It looks empty. But inside? Racks of clothes, shelves of toys, food, books — and it's all free.

That's the New Orleans Free Store. It used to be a Family Dollar in the Lower Ninth Ward. Hurricane Katrina hit this neighborhood more than 20 years ago, and many buildings were never fixed. Dan Bingler, who is 42, made a deal with the building's owner to use it rent-free. He only pays the bills. Three years ago, he turned it into a free store.

Twice a week, people line up outside. When the doors open, they rush in. Ernestine Lane shops there with a friend from church. "There's blessings in there, go in," she says.

Kids love it too. Angela, 8, found animal-print hair clips for school. Her sister Gloria, 9, picked up a furry vest to give to a baby her stepmom babysits.

The store also offers free STI testing, food handouts, art classes, and punk shows. And on Wednesday nights, the lights go dim and people roller skate on the polished floor.

Bingler thinks other empty stores around the country could do the same thing.
why_it_matters: It shows that one person with an empty building can turn it into something that helps a whole neighborhood, and kids can copy the idea in small ways, like a free swap table at school.

background_read: Hurricane Katrina was a giant storm that hit the U.S. Gulf Coast in 2005 and flooded most of New Orleans, a big city in the state of Louisiana.
The Lower Ninth Ward (a neighborhood in New Orleans) was one of the hardest-hit areas, and many homes and shops there were never rebuilt.
A 'free store' is a place where people can take what they need and give what they don't, without paying any money.
Article_Structure: WHO: Dan Bingler, a 42-year-old man who runs the New Orleans Free Store, plus shoppers like Ernestine Lane and kids Angela, 8, and Gloria, 9.
WHAT: An old Family Dollar store in the Lower Ninth Ward became a free store where clothes, toys, food and books cost nothing, and it also hosts art classes, punk shows and Wednesday roller skating.
WHERE: The Lower Ninth Ward in New Orleans, inside a graffiti-covered building that was never fixed after Hurricane Katrina.
WHY: Bingler wants to help a neighborhood that was never repaired — and he thinks other empty stores around the country could do the same thing.

perspectives.description: People like Ernestine Lane say the store is full of 'blessings' — it gives families free clothes, food and toys when money is tight.
Some people might wonder how a store can give everything away, or worry that one man paying all the bills means it might not last long.
Bingler believes the idea can spread, because other empty stores around the country could open their doors the same way.
